Yellow
yĕl'ō
adj. (of the colour of gold; in the law a diagnostic sign of leprosy in the hair, and in the Psalms the colour of a redeemed people's wings)
Old English geolu, akin to gold and to Latin helvus, pale yellow. The Hebrew tsahob is the sallow yellow of diseased hair; charuts in Psalm 68 is the yellow of refined gold.

Biblical Definition

The word runs at both ends of the scale. In Leviticus 13 it is a symptom the priest is trained to look for: “if it be in sight deeper than the skin; and there be in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard” (Lev 13:30). The examination is patient and exact — if after seven days “the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair” (Lev 13:32), the man is not condemned; but if the scall has spread, “the priest shall not seek for yellow hair; he is unclean” (Lev 13:36), because spreading has already settled the case. Then Psalm 68 takes the same colour for glory: “Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold” (Psa 68:13). A people blackened in the ash of the kitchen — slaves in Egypt, sleeping among the pots — are to shine like a dove in the sun. Between the two lies the whole gospel: the same eye that examines the sallow hair covers the redeemed with gold.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines yellow as being of a bright saffron color, or of the colour of gold; and notes it among the primary colours of the rainbow.

expand to see more

YELLOW, a. Being of a bright saffron color, or of a color partaking of that of gold.

There be in it a yellow thin hair. Lev. xiii.

YELLOW, n. A bright color, reflecting more light than any other except white.

YELLOWNESS, n. The quality of being yellow.

Key Scripture

Lev 13:30 — "Then the priest shall see the plague: and, behold, if it be in sight deeper than the skin; and there be in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard."

Lev 13:32 — "And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the plague: and, behold, if the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair, and the scall be not in sight deeper than the skin;"

Lev 13:36 — "Then the priest shall look on him: and, behold, if the scall be spread in the skin, the priest shall not seek for yellow hair; he is unclean."

Psa 68:13 — "Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold."

Modern Corruption

Leviticus 13 is dismissed as primitive medicine, though its whole procedure is a lesson in patient, evidenced judgment rather than in hygiene.

expand to see more

The leprosy chapters are the standard example given when the law is called a relic of ancient superstition, and the charge misses what the chapter is doing. The priest is not a physician prescribing a cure; he is an appointed examiner rendering a verdict about a man's standing in the congregation. And the procedure is remarkable for its restraint. He looks; if the evidence is ambiguous he shuts the man up seven days and looks again; if there is no spreading and no yellow hair, the man is pronounced clean and washes his clothes. Only a spreading plague settles the matter. The whole apparatus is a rebuke to hasty judgment in the church — a verdict rendered on stated evidence, after a set interval, by a man under authority, with an explicit provision for finding the accused clean.

The other half of the word supplies the mercy the chapter cannot. The leper of Leviticus 13:45 goes with rent clothes and covered lip crying Unclean, unclean, and there is nothing in the law that makes him otherwise. Psalm 68 sings of a people who lay among the pots — the phrase suggests the sooty ash by a kitchen fire, or the brick-kilns of Egypt — and says they shall be as a dove's wings covered with silver and her feathers with yellow gold. The transformation is entirely one-sided. The dove does not scrub herself into brightness; she is covered. Where the modern corruption speaks of self-improvement and the recovery of one's own dignity, Scripture speaks of a covering given to those who had none, and the New Testament names it: the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsahob (H6669), yellow, of diseased hair; charuts (H2742), sharpened, hence refined gold, in Psalm 68:13; netheq (H5424), the scall of Leviticus 13.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsahob (H6669) — yellow, golden-sallow; used only of the hair in the scall; Leviticus 13:30, Leviticus 13:32.

Hebrew netheq (H5424) — a scall, a scab of the head or beard; the specific plague examined; Leviticus 13:30.

Hebrew charuts (H2742) — gold, from a root meaning sharpened or refined; her feathers with yellow gold; Psalm 68:13.

Hebrew tame (H2931) — unclean; the priest's verdict, and the cry of the leper himself; Leviticus 13:45.

Hebrew yownah (H3123) — a dove; the figure of the covered and shining people; Psalm 68:13.

Usage

"“A yellow thin hair… the priest shall pronounce him unclean” — a verdict on stated evidence."

"“The priest shall not seek for yellow hair” — spreading has already settled it."

"“Her feathers with yellow gold” — a people out of the ash pits, covered."
